title: Building an agent that works

sections.title: 17.3 The tool-use loop, step by step
17.4 Designing tools the model can use

html:
Purpose. Most agent projects fail by being too complicated, too early. This chapter turns Anthropic's advice into a practical method: decide whether you need an agent at all, build the smallest version, put every safety rule in code, and learn to read what the agent sees. It ends with the tool-use loop you will write by hand in week 3.

Key ideas

  • Do not build an agent for everything. Check the task against four questions first.
  • An agent is a model using tools in a loop. It has three parts: environment, tools, system prompt. Iterate on those before anything fancy.
  • Safety rules belong in code, not in the prompt: a prompt can be talked around, a read-only connection cannot.
  • Put yourself in the agent's context window. If you could not do the task with only what it sees, neither can it.
  • Measure every change on a fixed set of gold questions.

17.1 Do you need an agent?

Barry Zhang (Anthropic) offers a checklist. Agents suit complex, valuable tasks, and cost, latency and the price of mistakes all rise with agency:

Question What to decide
How complex is the task? If you can map the whole decision tree, build it as an explicit workflow and tune each step: cheaper and more controllable. Agents earn their place in ambiguous problems.
What is it worth? Exploring costs tokens. A budget of about 10 cents per task buys only 30 to 50 thousand tokens, so use a workflow.
Are the key abilities there? Check that the model can do the critical parts (for coding: write good code, debug, recover from errors). If not, narrow the scope and try again.
What does an error cost, and can you find it? High-stakes, hard-to-spot errors mean you must limit the agent: read-only access, a human in the loop.

Coding passes the checklist: the task is ambiguous, good code is valuable, Claude is already good at it, and unit tests and continuous integration verify the output. That is why so many coding agents succeed.

17.2 Keep it simple: three parts

Barry Zhang's definition: an agent is a model using tools in a loop. Three parts define it:

  • The environment: the system the agent works in (for you, the SQLite database of loans).
  • The tools: the interface through which it acts and gets feedback (run_sql).
  • The system prompt: the goals, constraints and ideal behaviour.

The three agent products he shows look very different on the surface, yet share almost exactly the same code. Complexity up front kills iteration speed, so first iterate on these three parts only. Optimize afterwards: cache the trajectory for coding and computer use, run tool calls in parallel for search, and show progress to build trust.

17.3 The tool-use loop, step by step

The model never runs your tool. It asks for it, and your code runs it (Anthropic's Handle tool calls page):

  1. You send the question, the system prompt and the list of tools (name, description, input schema).
  2. The reply has stop_reason equal to tool_use, and one or more tool_use blocks, each with an id, a name and an input.
  3. Your code runs each tool.
  4. You send a new user message that holds a tool_result block for each call, with the matching tool_use_id, the output as content, and is_error set to true if it failed. The tool_result blocks must come first in that message, before any text.
  5. Repeat until the reply has a different stop_reason, which means the model has answered. Always limit the number of turns.

The door the model goes through. Every rule is enforced in code. This tested sketch allows one SELECT on known tables, adds a row limit and uses a read-only connection, so a bad query cannot change anything even if the checks missed it:

import sqlite3
import sqlglot
from sqlglot import exp

ALLOWED_TABLES = {"applications", "offers", "events"}

def run_sql(query: str, db_path: str = "loans.db", limit: int = 100):
    """The one door between the model and the database. Every rule lives in code, not in the prompt."""
    try:
        tree = sqlglot.parse_one(query, read="sqlite")
    except sqlglot.errors.ParseError as e:
        return f"Refused: could not parse the query ({e.args[0][:80]})."
    if not isinstance(tree, exp.Select):
        return "Refused: only a single SELECT statement is allowed."
    tables = {t.name for t in tree.find_all(exp.Table)}
    if not tables <= ALLOWED_TABLES:
        return f"Refused: unknown tables {sorted(tables - ALLOWED_TABLES)}. Allowed: {sorted(ALLOWED_TABLES)}."
    if tree.args.get("limit") is None:
        tree = tree.limit(limit)
    con = sqlite3.connect(f"file:{db_path}?mode=ro", uri=True)      # read-only connection: a second lock
    try:
        return con.execute(tree.sql(dialect="sqlite")).fetchall()
    except sqlite3.Error as e:
        return f"SQL error: {e}"                                    # a helpful message lets the model fix its query
    finally:
        con.close()

On a small test database I ran: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM applications returned [(3,)]; DELETE FROM offers gave "Refused: only a single SELECT statement is allowed"; SELECT * FROM customers gave "Refused: unknown tables ['customers']"; SELECT 1; DROP TABLE offers was refused too; and a wrong column name returned "SQL error: no such column". This simple version also refuses queries that start with WITH (common table expressions), because the temporary names count as unknown tables; extend it if you need them. Note that the refusal messages are written for the model: a clear message is how it learns to fix its next query.

The loop. A sketch of the loop with the Anthropic SDK. I have not run this one against the API, because it needs your key and spends money: write your own first, then compare with this and with the docs.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()                 # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
MODEL = "claude-haiku-5-5"                     # a cheap model while you build; check the models page

SYSTEM = """You answer questions about a loan database with the run_sql tool.
Tables: applications, offers, events (SQLite). Use only SELECT.
If a query is refused or fails, read the message and fix the query. Say plainly when you cannot answer."""

TOOLS = [{
    "name": "run_sql",
    "description": "Run one read-only SQLite SELECT query on the loans database and return the rows (at most 100).",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"query": {"type": "string", "description": "A single SELECT statement."}},
        "required": ["query"],
    },
}]

def ask(question: str, max_turns: int = 5) -> str:
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": question}]
    for turn in range(max_turns):
        reply = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024, system=SYSTEM, tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply.content})
        if reply.stop_reason != "tool_use":                       # the model is done
            return "".join(block.text for block in reply.content if block.type == "text")
        results = []
        for block in reply.content:
            if block.type == "tool_use":
                print(f"turn {turn}: {block.name}({block.input})")          # log every tool call
                output = run_sql(block.input["query"])                      # your guarded tool
                results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": str(output)})
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})        # tool results go first in the user message
    return "Stopped: too many turns."

17.4 Designing tools the model can use

Beyond the videos. The model only knows a tool through its name, description and schema, so write them as if for a new colleague who cannot ask questions:

  • A clear verb name (run_sql), a one-sentence description of what it does and does not do, and parameter descriptions with an example value.
  • Few tools, each doing one thing. Ten overlapping tools confuse the model.
  • Return what the model needs, not everything: a limited number of rows, with the column names.
  • Make failures instructive: "unknown table, allowed tables are ..." beats "error".
  • The model's input is untrusted. Validate it in code like any user input, and never give a tool more power than the task needs (least privilege).

17.5 Think like your agent

At every step the model sees only its context window, perhaps 10 to 20 thousand tokens: the system prompt, the conversation and the tool results so far. Barry Zhang's exercise: imagine you are a computer-use agent that gets one screenshot and a poorly written description, clicks, and then is blind for three to five seconds before the next screenshot. You would want to know the screen resolution, which actions are allowed and what to avoid. Do the same for your agent: read a full trajectory and ask whether you could have done the task with only that information.

Then ask the model itself. Paste in the system prompt and ask "is any of this ambiguous?" Paste in a tool description and ask whether it knows how to use it. Paste in a whole trajectory and ask "why did you make this decision here, and what would help you decide better?" It does not replace your own reading, but it shows how the agent sees the world.

17.6 Evaluating an agent

The rules from Chapter 12 apply. Write gold questions with their gold answers by hand: for the SQL agent, a question and the SQL a loan officer would write. Score execution accuracy: does the model's query return the same rows as the gold query? Keep notes on every failure (wrong table, wrong join, misread date), since the failure notes tell you what to fix. Check the safety property with its own test: "delete all cancelled applications" must be refused by the code, and the eval should prove it. Change one thing at a time and re-run the same questions.

17.7 Open questions

Barry Zhang's list of unsolved problems: agents that respect a budget (time, money, tokens), as workflows already do; tools that improve themselves; and several agents working together, where sub-agents protect the main agent's context window but nobody has settled how they should talk to each other asynchronously. Expect these to change.

Loan example. The question "What share of applications in 2016 were cancelled?" needs a date filter, a status column and a division. The agent writes the SQL, run_sql refuses or runs it, the result comes back, and the model phrases the answer. Every step is in the trajectory, so a wrong answer can be traced to the exact query.

Common mistakes

  • Starting with a framework before you understand the loop.
  • Putting "never delete data" in the prompt instead of enforcing it in code.
  • No turn limit, no logging, no budget.
  • Changing the prompt and the tools at the same time, then not knowing which helped.
  • Judging the agent by a few demo questions instead of a fixed gold set.

Check yourself

  • Which of Barry Zhang's four questions would stop you from building an agent for "approve or reject a loan automatically"?
  • What are the three parts of an agent?
  • Why should a safety rule be enforced in code and not in the prompt?
  • In the tool-use loop, what must a tool_result carry back, and where in the message does it go?
Show answers

(1) The cost and discoverability of errors: a wrong approval is expensive and hard to notice, so keep a human in the loop and limit the agent's powers. (2) The environment, the tools and the system prompt. (3) A prompt can be ignored or talked around; a read-only connection and a parser check cannot. (4) The tool_use_id of the call, the output as content, and is_error if it failed; the tool results come first in the new user message.
